evidence.claim: In August 2011, Tropical Storm Irene destroyed sections of Route 100 between Killington and Bethel, preventing vehicle travel into and out of Pittsfield for weeks.
evidence.quote: In August 2011, Pittsfield became known as one of the most isolated Vermont towns when Tropical Storm Irene destroyed parts of Vermont Route 100 between Killington and Bethel, preventing vehicle travel in and out of the town for weeks.

evidence.claim: The state subsequently reconstructed many segments of Route 100 damaged by the storm.
evidence.quote: since that storm, the state has undertaken the reconstruction of many segments of the road.

evidence.claim: Chartered as Killington in 1761, the town became Sherburne in 1800, taking the name of landholder Colonel Benjamin Sherburne.
evidence.quote: The town of Killington was chartered on July 7, 1761, by a New Hampshire grant. In 1800, it was renamed Sherburne after landholder Colonel Benjamin Sherburne.

evidence.claim: Voters chose the original name again in March 1999, and legislative approval made the change effective that July.
evidence.quote: The town voted to revert to its original name of Killington on March 2, 1999; which was approved by the Vermont General Assembly and became effective July 1, 1999.

evidence.claim: Killington Road connects US 4 with the ski area through the central village.
evidence.quote: The central part of the town, extending along Killington Road from U.S. Route 4 in the north to the Killington Ski Resort in the south, comprises the Killington Village census-designated place.

evidence.claim: A family parlor became the setting for a presidential oath at the Coolidge Homestead.
evidence.quote: Coolidge was sworn in by his father in the family parlor

evidence.claim: Calvin Coolidge was visiting his family here when President Warren G. Harding died.
evidence.quote: Calvin Coolidge often returned to the homestead to visit his family, and he was staying there when President Warren G. Harding died.

evidence.claim: His father administered the oath in the house where Coolidge had lived from age four until leaving for Black River Academy in 1887.
evidence.quote: Coolidge lived there from age four in 1876 to 1887, when he departed for Black River Academy for education.

evidence.claim: His father’s refusal to modernize the house preserved its condition and some furnishings from that night.
evidence.quote: Due to his father's refusal to modernize the house it remains in the same condition, and in some cases with the same furnishings, as it was the night Coolidge took the oath.

evidence.claim: The inaugural room’s lamp, Bible and table occupy their historic positions behind glass.
evidence.quote: The Inaugural Room itself is behind glass, but a visitor can stand in an alcove and see the lamp, Bible, and table that were used in the ceremony, all placed in their historic positions.

evidence.claim: Ludlow’s three-story brick woolen mill replaced a taller building lost to fire.
evidence.quote: The original building, which was five stories tall, burned in 1865 and was rebuilt as the three-story brick building that remains today.

evidence.claim: The first mill opened in 1834, failed during the panic of 1837 and resumed production by 1853.
evidence.quote: The mill was first built for woolen manufacture in 1834 and operated until 1837, when the business failed in the economic panic of that year. After sitting vacant for a time, it was sold and had resumed operation by 1853.

evidence.claim: After the 1865 fire came the brick replacement that survives in the village.
evidence.quote: The original building, which was five stories tall, burned in 1865 and was rebuilt as the three-story brick building that remains today.

evidence.claim: By 1899, the company employed 130 people and produced 150,000 yards of wool cloth a year.
evidence.quote: In 1899, it employed 130 people and produced 150,000 yards of wool cloth annually.

evidence.claim: The former mill now houses a condominium and retail businesses within the Ludlow Village Historic District.
evidence.quote: includes the former Ludlow Woolen Mills (now housing a condominium and several retail businesses)
